lines.text: Five hundred and twenty five days.
That's how long South Africa has gone without load shedding, says Eskom.
That's about seventeen months, counting from the sixteenth of May 2025.
Many of us remember sitting in the dark for hours, so this feels almost unreal.
So how did Eskom do it? And what is still not fixed? Let's open the case.
Case file: how Eskom kept the lights on.
Meet Mama Zinhle. She is an example, not a real person.
She runs a small spaza shop in Soweto.
In the bad years, load shedding meant her fridge went off and her stock went bad.
Now her lights have stayed on for more than a year.
But she still asks: is this really over, or just a good patch?
First, a quick look back.
Load shedding began in late 2007, and got much worse in the late 2010s and early 2020s.
In July 2022, President Ramaphosa launched the Energy Action Plan.
Between March 2024 and January 2025, the country went ten months without load shedding, but then it came back.
In April and May 2025, there were twenty six hours of cuts, spread over four days.
Since the sixteenth of May 2025, there have been none.
And on the fifteenth of May 2026, we passed the first full year without load shedding since September 2018.
Here are the headline numbers, from Eskom's own statement on the twenty third of October.
Five hundred and twenty five days in a row with no load shedding.
Eskom says sixty eight point one percent of its power was ready to work this financial year so far, which is the best in six years.
A year ago, over the same stretch, it was about sixty two and a half percent.
And Eskom says it has almost five thousand megawatts spare above what the country is using right now. Megawatts, or M W, is how we measure power.
Now, what are people asking?
These are common questions, not quotes from one person.
Many people ask: is Eskom just telling us what we want to hear?
Others ask: why is my power still off sometimes?
And almost everyone asks: will my bill finally stop going up?
So how did it happen? There are three big things.
One: fixing the old power stations on purpose.
Two: bringing back units that were stuck for years.
And three: rooftop solar on homes and businesses, which isn't Eskom's own work, but helped.
Cause one: servicing the fleet on purpose.
Think of Eskom's power stations as a taxi rank.
In 2023, about one in three taxis was broken down or stuck in the workshop.
So Eskom did something that looks odd: it took even more taxis off the road for proper servicing, about eight thousand megawatts on average in summer 2023.
Priority stations included Tutuka, Duvha, Majuba, Matla, Kendal, Arnot, Kriel and Koeberg.
In April 2023, about eighteen thousand megawatts were broken down.
By April 2025, that was down to about thirteen thousand.
Cause two: bringing back units that were stuck for years.
In March 2025, Kusile Unit 6 was connected to the grid, adding eight hundred megawatts.
In July 2025, Medupi Unit 4 came back, after a generator exploded in 2021.
And in October 2025, Koeberg Unit 1 was reconnected, adding nine hundred and thirty megawatts.
Eskom says about seven thousand eight hundred megawatts have been restored since 2023, from finished long repairs and new units.
Cause three: rooftop solar.
Meet Mr Pillay, an example from Durban who put panels on his roof.
Many homes and businesses did the same, and reports say this helped South Africa pass a year without load shedding.
But solar isn't perfect, because clouds cut how much power panels make.
Eskom says the grid stayed stable this winter, even when heavy overcast skies cut rooftop solar.
We don't have a number for how much solar helped, so we won't guess.
So what did all that fixing and restarting do?
Eskom says that three years ago, about sixteen thousand megawatts were broken down at any time.
Now it is about nine thousand one hundred.
That's a drop of seven thousand and sixty four megawatts.
Compared with last year, that's about three thousand megawatts fewer breakdowns.
Careful: these are Eskom's own numbers, from the twenty third of October, and they move a little each week.
There's money news too.
Eskom uses diesel to make power when other plants fall short, and diesel is expensive.
Last year, over the same stretch, it spent six point oh seven billion rand on diesel.
This year, it's one point two six billion rand.
That's four point eight one billion rand saved, almost eighty percent less.
That is a saving of nearly five billion rand in one year.
And the figure moves. On the second of October the saving was four point seven nine billion.
Now the honest question: can we trust these numbers?
The availability number and the 525 days are Eskom's own measures.
A website called GridPulse rebuilt the figures from the hourly data Eskom publishes for its stations, and got sixty eight percent.
That agrees with Eskom, but it still uses Eskom's data.
And we found no outside audit of the availability or breakdown numbers.
Here's the catch. Meet Sipho, an example from a Gauteng township.
His power goes off at five in the morning, and again in the evening.
He asks: Eskom says no load shedding, so what is this?
Good question. This is load reduction, and it is not the same as load shedding.
Load shedding is national, rotating cuts when there isn't enough power.
Load reduction is local. Eskom says it protects equipment from overloading, in areas with illegal connections or overloaded networks.
Eskom says seven provinces are free of it.
The rest is limited to selected areas in Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal.
The Citizen's Gauteng schedule this week shows cuts from five to nine in the morning, and five to ten at night.
So the national problem is fixed, but the local one is not.
What else is not fixed?
Sixty eight percent ready also means about thirty two percent is not.
Some of that is planned servicing, and some is still breakdowns, about nine thousand megawatts of it.
Eskom's winter update says breakdowns fell from about thirty four percent of its capacity to about nineteen and a half.
That's still about one in five taxis broken down.
And this can slip. After ten months of light in 2024, the cuts came back in 2025.
What does this mean for your pocket?
Lights on is not the same as a cheaper bill.
The regulator, NERSA, decides how much Eskom can charge, and it approved eight point seven six percent more for Eskom's direct customers from the first of April 2026.
It also approved nine point oh one percent more for municipalities from the first of July. A municipality is your local council, which buys power from Eskom in bulk.
So bills are still rising, but shops, workshops and homes can plan their days around power that stays on.
So, the verdict.
The evidence points to servicing and restarted units, with rooftop solar helping.
But the main numbers are Eskom's own, and we found no outside audit.
And local cuts, breakdowns and rising bills are still with us.
You don't have to take anyone's word for it. Here's how to check.
One. Look at the date on any Eskom number, because they change from week to week.
Two. Ask who measured it. Is it Eskom's own figure, or someone else's?
Three. Compare with GridPulse, a website that rebuilds the numbers from Eskom's published data.
Four. Keep your own record. How many times did your power go off this month?
So what can you do?
One. Learn the difference between load shedding, which is national, and load reduction, which is local.
Two. Check the schedule for your area, so local cuts don't surprise you.
Three. Don't add illegal connections, and talk to your neighbours about it, because overloaded networks are why some areas get cut.
Four. Plan for higher bills, because tariffs went up this year.
And five. Keep your candles and power bank for now, because after ten months of light, the cuts came back in 2025.
Has the power stayed on in your area? Tell us in the comments.
Follow Pulse SA News, and share this with someone who still remembers the dark days.
